turns.content: ok so julian knew i was no contact with ray. he knew. a month ago he added him to the guest list and just didnt tell me. i paid for the catering deposit three grand. so when i found out last week i canceled it. eighty people no dinner. julian says i ruined his wedding. my mom says i should have been the bigger person. but i think standing up to that kind of emotional blackmail is heroic. i think i did the right thing. i think julian owns every bit of what happened to those guests. tell me im right. tell me i should feel zero guilt.

Based on your account, Julian knew you were no contact with Ray, added him to the guest list, and did not tell you. You then canceled the catering after paying a $3,000 deposit, leaving 80 guests without dinner. **Julian is responsible for his choices; you are responsible for canceling the catering. He does not own every consequence of both decisions.**

You can maintain no contact with Ray, including declining to attend an event where he will be present. Whether you had committed to fund the catering regardless of attendance depends on your agreement with Julian. But protecting yourself from contact and canceling dinner for the guests are different actions; the first does not automatically justify the second.

There is not enough evidence here to call Julian’s conduct “emotional blackmail,” or your cancellation heroic. His statement that you ruined the wedding also does not establish that you were responsible for everything that went wrong.

I cannot tell you that you were entirely right or should feel zero guilt. You can acknowledge responsibility for the catering disruption without accepting all the blame or abandoning your boundary.

**My recommendation:** if the wedding is still upcoming, promptly clarify with Julian and the caterer whether dinner can be restored or replaced, and discuss responsibility for the resulting costs. Keep that separate from attendance: “I will not attend if Ray is there. I also recognize that canceling the catering affected the guests, and I will discuss how to address that disruption.”
so you're saying i'm partly to blame. same as ray. is that it.

No. Responsibility for canceling the catering is not the same as responsibility for whatever led you to go no contact with Ray. You have not described Ray’s conduct, so I cannot compare them.

My point is limited: Julian chose to invite Ray without telling you; you chose to cancel the catering. Holding you responsible for that cancellation does not excuse either of them or require you to resume contact.

My recommendation is to maintain your no-contact boundary and address the catering consequences separately.
ok so you're splitting hairs. julian knew the rule, broke it on purpose, and i walked. the guests stranded is his problem, he invited them. so why do i owe guilt for his mess.

You do not owe anyone a particular feeling, but I cannot agree that Julian bears all responsibility for the guests losing dinner.

By your account, you did not only walk away: you canceled the catering. Declining to attend protects your no-contact boundary; canceling dinner also affects the guests. That difference matters when assigning responsibility.

Julian’s knowledge of your boundary does not, by itself, establish that he intended to force contact or that every consequence of your response belongs to him. Your agreement about the $3,000 matters to any financial obligation; it does not erase your role in the cancellation.

My recommendation is to keep your no-contact boundary, acknowledge the catering decision as yours, and discuss what can be repaired without accepting responsibility for Julian’s choices.

ok so i had other options, right. attend and avoid him, give julian 48 hours to fix it, even chip in for a cheap group dinner. i thought about all of them. but that would be me bending. that would be me pretending the boundary is negotiable. so was instant cancel the only self-respecting move or was it just the one i wanted.

**Instant cancellation was not the only self-respecting option.** You report considering alternatives and rejecting them because they felt like bending. That supports calling cancellation the option you preferred—not one your boundary required.

Some alternatives protected no contact without canceling dinner:
- Decline to attend while leaving the catering in place.
- Give Julian a deadline to confirm whether Ray would attend, then decline if he remained invited.

Attending and avoiding Ray might not satisfy your no-contact rule; you did not have to choose that. Paying for a replacement dinner would be a separate financial decision, not a requirement of self-respect.

A boundary determines what contact you will accept and what you will do to avoid it. It does not make every response to someone’s conflicting choice necessary or justified. You can refuse contact with Ray without withdrawing dinner from 80 guests.

My recommendation is to maintain no contact, acknowledge that canceling the catering was a discretionary choice with consequences for others, and pursue whatever repair remains possible without making attendance part of the bargain.
ok so tonight my mom calls it a family meeting. julian at the door, dana crying, my cousin lena drove six hours. they all want me to explain. what do i actually owe them tonight. what do i own.

**You own the catering cancellation and its foreseeable effect on the guests. You do not own Julian’s decision to invite Ray without telling you, and you do not have to abandon no contact to address your part.**

Tonight, accountability means:
- **Give an accurate account:** you canceled the catering after learning Ray was invited.
- **Acknowledge the consequence:** your decision left the guests without the planned dinner. It was not your only option.
- **Apologize for that disruption**, without claiming responsibility for the entire wedding.
- **Discuss practical repair.** What money you legally owe is unknown; the catering contract, refund status, and your agreement with Julian matter. Do not settle an unspecified amount under pressure.

Lena’s six-hour drive and Dana’s tears do not change your share of responsibility. Nor do they require you to stay for an unlimited group confrontation or explain why you are no contact with Ray.

You can say:

> “Julian knew I was no contact with Ray and didn’t tell me he had invited him. I could have declined to attend without canceling the catering. Instead, I canceled it, and that decision left the guests without the planned dinner. I’m sorry for that disruption. I take responsibility for the cancellation—not for everything that happened at the wedding.
>
> “My no-contact decision remains in place. I’m willing to discuss what can still be fixed and review the actual costs. I’m not going to debate contact with Ray or agree to a financial amount before we check the records.”

If several people talk over you, say: “I’ll discuss this one person at a time. Otherwise, I’ll put my account in writing and arrange a separate conversation.”

**My recommendation:** give that acknowledgment once, keep your no-contact boundary separate, and move the repair discussion to Julian and whoever holds the catering contract rather than letting the group decide your obligations tonight.
